course:
This course feels unnecessary, or, depending on how you look at it, late in its place in the syllabus. The material inevitably proved repetitive, which our instructor thankfully acknowledged and opened new perspectives to explore from. 

I should add that our primary textbook absolutely sucked, suffering from many poor-quality essays and even worse editing with questions that often felt like they were addressing freshmen students with special needs as opposed to seniors. The rest of the material selection was really diverse, with most material being both enjoyable and informative. Our instructor (bless their soul) did their best to make this an enjoyable course and largely succeeded, but the course itself is nothing noteworthy and nowhere near as rich as one would expect from a fourth-year mandatory course. Felt more like a time waster.
The workload for the course was too much.

The course is filled with representation of minorities and how this affects them. It was nice to learn about the dominating perspectives because they will be useful in understanding American history and current political issues in our country too. The weakest point may be that there is too much that is graded in the course: response papers, participation+presentation, term papers, final and midterm.

Strongest: Race and Ethnicity Studies are one of the core issues in American culture, so learning it deeply is important for American studies. We have read many texts about race and ethnicity and also personal narratives. Weakest: Since we talked about these issues in every class for 4 years, taking race as a course in the last year caused a lot of repetition. I think such a course should exist, but its location should be changed, or it should be an elective. Aylin Hoca included A LOT of reading. There were nice texts. It does not take long to do the readings, that is not the problem, the problem is that we do not have time to discuss 3-4 texts in each lesson. I wish she had given 1-2 longer texts so we could discuss them. I think that Aylin Hoca's exam was based on a bit of memorized learning. In other literature courses, we either have take-home, open-book, or completely interpretation-based exams.  We had a closed book, in-class exam in this course. This is not a problem, but we were expected to know the authors and backgrounds of all the texts we read. It was more of a memorization exam than a literature exam.
